THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Ten early traces of hominin activity

A line of footprints, a struck flake and a sliced animal bone each preserve a different kind of action. Ten localities show how archaeologists read those traces, estimate their ages and ask which hominins left them.

Ten selected very early activity localities in Africa and Asia. The sequence compares evidence types and approximate ages. Overlapping age brackets preclude a definitive global ranking, and the finds record activity ranging from a brief crossing to repeated use of a landscape.

How to read an early trace

Footprints document movement across a surface. Refitted flakes and cores preserve parts of a stoneworking sequence. Cut marks and wear can connect tools to activities such as carcass processing. A fossil hominin records a body, while attribution of a nearby artifact to its species requires additional evidence. [1] [17] [4]

Ma means million years ago. Dates refer to the ancient track, object-bearing deposit or earliest dated horizon described in each guide. Some ages are central estimates within wide ranges. [1] [14]

Stoneworking before the earliest known Homo

Lomekwi 3’s stone artifacts are older than the oldest fossil currently assigned to Homo. Nyayanga’s Oldowan layers include Paranthropus teeth, and Namorotukunan preserves early Oldowan horizons across changes in its landscape. The molecular and anatomical evidence needed to assign the tools to a particular species is usually absent. [3] [18] [4] [5]

At Dikika, researchers reported two animal bones with marks they interpreted as evidence of butchery more than 3.39 million years ago. Other kinds of damage can mimic tool marks, and no tools were recovered with those bones. The two marked bones are discussed here as a disputed line of evidence. [19] [20]

Comparing traces across regions

The long sequence at Shangchen documents repeated presence in central China. Dmanisi independently records an early dispersal with both tools and hominin remains. And Lokalalei 2C in Kenya, roughly contemporary with the early Shungura record, is especially informative about the production of flakes because pieces can be refitted. [15] [21] [17] [14]

  • Lucy and her world — A 3.2-million-year-old skeleton from Hadar, and the fossils and footprints that help explain how her species moved.
  • The branching human family — From late Miocene candidates to Homo sapiens, Neanderthals and Denisovans, with the places where the earliest evidence was found.
  • Laetoli footprint trails — Footprints in volcanic ash document upright walking about 3.66 million years ago.
  • Lomekwi 3 — Large flaked and battered stones from western Lake Turkana date to about 3.3 million years ago.
  • Nyayanga — Early Oldowan artifacts, processed animal bones and Paranthropus teeth occur on Kenya’s Homa Peninsula.
  • Namorotukunan — Three Oldowan horizons in the northeastern Turkana Basin record toolmaking from about 2.75 to 2.44 million years ago.
  • Bokol Dora 1, Ledi-Geraru — Early Oldowan flaking in Ethiopia’s Afar dates to about 2.61–2.58 million years ago.
  • Gona Oldowan localities — Several Afar localities preserve some of the best studied Oldowan tools from around 2.6 million years ago.
  • Aïn Boucherit — Stone artifacts and butchered bones near Sétif preserve early hominin activity in northern Africa.
  • Hadar’s Makaamitalu localities — A younger part of the Hadar sequence preserves Oldowan tools and a maxilla of early Homo.
  • Lower Omo, Shungura Formation — Early stone scatters document toolmaking along the lower Omo at about 2.33 million years ago.
  • Shangchen, Chinese Loess Plateau — Tool-bearing layers in Shaanxi document early activity outside Africa from about 2.12 million years ago.
  • Before 1 Million Years Ago: Every Global Hominin & Tool Site (7.0–1.0 Ma) — Exhaustive planetary inventory of 164 hominin fossil and archaeological localities dated older than 1.0 Ma across Africa, the Levant, Caucasus, Europe, Asia, and oceanic Wallacea—plus species attributions and dispersal routes.
  • Australopithecus: Every Published Fossil Locality Across Africa — Complete species-by-species and basin-by-basin catalogue of 39 published Australopithecus fossil localities across East, Central (Chad), and Southern Africa (~5.0–1.98 Ma).
